segments.say: Everything in this video so far has been about the ordinary path of recovery: friends, time, writing, meaning, small routines. For most people, that is enough, or enough with a little extra support. But for some people it isn't, and it's important to know the difference. Asking for professional help is not a failure of resilience. It's one of the things resilient people do.

It's worth saying clearly that pain by itself is not the sign that something is wrong. Intense sadness, fear and anger after a shock are normal. The signal that professional help may be needed is different. It's when the distress is not easing, when it's getting in the way of daily life, or when it's pushing the person toward harming themselves.

These are not a checklist for diagnosing yourself, and not all of them need to be present. If you recognise even one of them for more than a short while, it's a good reason to speak to a doctor or a mental health professional. If you're having thoughts of ending your life, please don't wait. Contact an emergency service or a crisis line in your country now. In the United States you can call or text 988. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, the Samaritans can be reached on 116 123. In other countries, a local doctor or emergency number can point you to help.

show.title: Signs it may be time to get help
items: Distress that is not easing after many weeks
Being unable to work, study or look after yourself
Nightmares, flashbacks or avoiding anything that reminds you
Using alcohol or drugs to get through the day
Thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life

segments.say: For some people who've lost someone, the grief doesn't soften. Instead it stays as intense as it was in the first weeks, with constant longing, difficulty accepting the death and a sense that life has no meaning, for a year or more. Researchers and clinicians have named this prolonged grief disorder, and it's now recognised in the major diagnostic manuals.

Holly Prigerson and a large group of colleagues tested proposed criteria for a grief disorder in several samples of bereaved people. They found that a distinct pattern of symptoms, mainly intense yearning, preoccupation with the person who died, and difficulty moving on, could be reliably identified, and that it was linked with impairment in daily life. This research contributed to the inclusion of prolonged grief disorder in the diagnostic system.

show.what: Prolonged grief disorder: psychometric validation of criteria proposed for DSM-V and ICD-11

segments.say: It's important to know that this condition, however distressing, responds to treatment. A specialised form of therapy was developed for it, and tested against a standard therapy for depression.

Katherine Shear and her colleagues randomly assigned adults with complicated grief to either a new treatment designed for grief or to a standard therapy for depression. About half of those who received the grief-focused treatment responded, compared with just over a quarter of those who received the standard therapy. The results suggested that grief that is stuck needs treatment aimed at grief itself, not only at depression.

show.what: Treatment of complicated grief: a randomized controlled trial

segments.say: The treatment does not ask a person to forget or to get over a loss. It helps them to carry it differently. It's a good example of the theme of this entire video: that the aim is to build a life that has room for what happened, not to return to the life that existed before.

show.title: What the grief treatment includes
items: Learning about grief and what keeps it stuck
Talking about the death, in a safe setting
Revisiting places and reminders gradually
Setting goals for a life that includes the loss

segments.say: Something similar applies to trauma. For most people, as we saw earlier, the first weeks are the worst, and things settle with time. But when nightmares, flashbacks and avoidance continue for months, the pattern may be post-traumatic stress disorder, and there are good treatments for it.

Rebekah Bradley and her colleagues combined the results of many studies of psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. They found that treatments that help people to gradually face memories and reminders of the trauma, together with changing unhelpful thoughts, led to substantial improvement for many patients, and that the gains were maintained over time.

show.what: A multidimensional meta-analysis of psychotherapy for PTSD

segments.say: You don't need to remember these names. The point is that effective help exists, and that a professional can tell you which one suits you. Good treatment is typically structured, time-limited and focused on the symptoms. It isn't an open-ended conversation about your past.

show.title: Treatments with good evidence for trauma
items: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy
Prolonged exposure therapy
Cognitive processing therapy
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing

segments.say: Starting is often the hardest part. A family doctor is a good first step in many countries. You can say something very simple, such as, I've been through something difficult and I'm not coping as I'd like. You don't need a perfect explanation. Many people find it helps to write down the main symptoms beforehand, and to bring a friend to the appointment.

Four terms from this chapter. Prolonged grief disorder is grief that stays intense for a year or more and interferes with life. Post-traumatic stress disorder is a pattern of intrusive memories, avoidance and arousal after trauma. Trauma-focused therapy is treatment that deals directly with the traumatic memory. And a crisis line is a service you can call at once when you're in danger. Picture this scene. A woman has been struggling since an accident two years ago. She tells herself that other people have had it worse and that she ought to manage. One day her sister notices that she has stopped driving and is sleeping badly, and gently suggests she see a doctor. The doctor listens, explains what she is describing, and refers her to a therapist. After a few months of structured treatment, the nightmares fade and she drives again. Looking back, she says that she wasted a year waiting to feel bad enough to ask. The research agrees that earlier help usually serves people better than later.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Prolonged grief disorder
Post-traumatic stress disorder
Trauma-focused therapy
Crisis line

segments.say: This video can't diagnose anyone, and it's not a substitute for professional care. But here is a simple way to think about it. Ask yourself how long it's been this heavy. Ask what it's stopping you from doing. Ask someone you trust what they've noticed, because people close to us often see changes before we do. And remember that asking for an assessment is not a commitment to anything. You can ask once, hear what the options are, and then decide. Most people who do this say afterwards that they wish they had done it sooner. It is one of the bravest and most sensible things a person can do, and it fits with everything that the research on resilience tells us. People get through hard things with help.

show.title: If you are unsure whether to ask for help
items: Ask yourself how long it has been this heavy
Ask what it is stopping you from doing
Ask a trusted person what they have noticed
Remember that you can ask once and then decide

segments.say: A window with a light on, and a door left open. That's what good help looks like at its best. Not an intervention, not a verdict, just a place that's lit and ready, where you can walk in when you decide that you're ready.

There's a quiet myth that needing help means that you were not strong enough. The research tells the opposite story. The people who recover best are usually the ones who allowed others in, who used what was available and who didn't wait for the pain to become unbearable. Reaching out is part of resilience, not a departure from it.

So what did we learn? That pain by itself is not the signal, but distress that doesn't ease is. That prolonged grief and trauma reactions are real and treatable. That specialised therapies work. And that asking for help is both sensible and brave.
In the last chapter, we'll bring all of this together, and look at what it means to live with a worldview that has been broken and rebuilt.
